description: Malaikah, al-Qadr and Muslim teaching on life after death — plus comparison with Christian afterlife.
content_html:
Malaikah: Angels in Islam

Malaikah (singular: malak) are angels — spiritual beings created by Allah from light (nur). They have no free will; they exist only to obey Allah. They are not depicted with wings or human form in Islamic theology, though the Qur’an uses figurative language. Angels are part of the unseen world (al-ghayb).

Three angels are named in the spec:

  • Jibril (Gabriel): the angel of revelation, through whom Allah communicated the Qur’an to Muhammad. Surah 2:97–98 states: “Whoever is an enemy of Jibril — it is he who has brought the Qur’an down upon your heart.” Jibril also appeared to Maryam to announce the birth of Isa.
  • Mika’il (Michael): the angel of sustenance and mercy, associated with rain, provision and natural phenomena that sustain life. Surah 2:98 mentions him alongside Jibril.
  • Izra’il: the angel of death, who takes the soul at the moment of death. Surah 32:11 states: “The angel of death who has been entrusted with you will take you, and then you will be returned to your Lord.” Izra’il serves as a reminder that death is controlled by Allah, not by chance.

The Qur’an also names Kiraman Katibin — the two recording angels assigned to every person, noting their deeds. These records will be opened on the Day of Judgement.

Key Fact

Three named angels: Jibril (revelation, Surah 2:97–98), Mika’il (sustenance, Surah 2:98), Izra’il (death, Surah 32:11). All are created from light, have no free will, and carry out Allah’s commands perfectly.

Al-Qadr: Predestination

Al-Qadr is the Arabic term for divine decree or predestination. Muslims believe that Allah has complete foreknowledge of all events and that nothing falls outside his will. The hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari 78:685 relates the Prophet Muhammad’s teaching that every human being is created with their fate ‘written’ by an angel before birth, including their provision, lifespan, deeds and whether they will enter paradise or the fire.

This doctrine is one of the Six Beliefs of Sunni Islam. It teaches that human beings are not independent agents operating outside Allah’s knowledge, but it does not eliminate human moral responsibility: Muslims are still judged on the basis of their choices.

Sunni and Shi’a approaches to predestination differ in emphasis:

  • Sunni Islam holds that al-Qadr is one of the Six Beliefs: Allah knows and decrees all things. Most Sunni theologians teach that both divine foreknowledge and genuine human free will coexist, though how this is possible is a theological mystery (taqdeer). Human beings choose and are accountable; Allah knows those choices in advance.
  • Shi’a Islam places greater emphasis on Adl (divine justice) as the governing principle. A just God would not predetermine a person’s actions and then punish them — therefore, humans must have genuine freedom. Shi’a theology generally stresses human free will more strongly than some Sunni accounts.

Akhirah: Life After Death

Akhirah means ‘the hereafter’ or ‘the afterlife.’ It encompasses the events that follow death: the intermediate state (barzakh), the resurrection, the Day of Judgement, and the final destinations of paradise (Jannah) or hell (Jahannam).

Surah 17:49–72 is the spec-named Qur’anic passage for Akhirah. It describes sceptics asking how God could resurrect decomposed bones, to which the answer is: “Say: Be you stones or iron, or [any] creation of that which is great within your breasts. And they will say, ‘Who will restore us?’ Say, ‘He who created you the first time.’” Allah, who created from nothing, can certainly resurrect the dead.

The sequence of events in Islamic eschatology:

  1. Death and Barzakh: After death the soul enters a waiting state (barzakh — the ‘barrier’ between this world and the Day of Judgement).
  2. Resurrection: On the Last Day, all souls are resurrected bodily.
  3. Judgement: Each person’s deeds are weighed on scales (mizan). The recording angels’ books are opened. Allah’s mercy also plays a decisive role — he may forgive those whose deeds are insufficient.
  4. Jannah or Jahannam: The righteous enter Jannah (paradise) — a garden of eternal bliss in the presence of Allah. The unrighteous enter Jahannam (hell) — a place of fire and separation from God.

This is the comparison-marked spec point (2C 1.8*):

  • Both traditions teach bodily resurrection, final judgement, paradise and a place of punishment. Both hold that earthly life shapes eternal destiny.
  • Islam: no purgatory or intermediate purification state (other than barzakh as a waiting state). Judgement is based on the weighing of deeds. The role of a mediating figure (like Christ in Christianity) is absent — Allah alone judges, though his mercy is decisive.
  • Christianity (Catholic): purgatory allows purification after death for those not fully ready for heaven. Salvation is achieved through faith in Christ, whose atoning death ‘pays’ for sin — a concept absent from Islam. Protestant Christianity rejects purgatory.
  • Key difference: Islamic judgement is more explicitly deed-based with direct divine mercy; Catholic Christianity builds in an intermediate purification stage and grounds salvation in Christ’s atonement.
Key Fact

Islamic eschatology sequence: death → barzakh (waiting state) → resurrection → judgement (deeds weighed on mizan) → Jannah (paradise) or Jahannam (hell). Surah 17:49–72 is the key Qur’anic passage on resurrection.
exam_tip_html: The 2C 1.8* marker means a 12-mark Discuss question comparing Muslim and Christian afterlife is very likely: “Islam and Christianity have the same beliefs about life after death.” The sharpest contrast is purgatory (Catholic Christianity) vs no purgatory (Islam); and atonement through Christ (Christianity) vs deed-based judgement with divine mercy (Islam). Develop both sides with named sources: Surah 17:49–72 for Islamic resurrection; 2 Corinthians 5:1–10 or the 39 Articles for Christian afterlife. For the 5-mark Explain on predestination, Sahih al-Bukhari 78:685 is the spec-named hadith — cite it as ‘Sahih al-Bukhari 78:685’ to earn the source mark. Do not write ‘a hadith says...’ without naming the collection. Correct spelling of ‘Akhirah’, ‘Malaikah’, ‘al-Qadr’ earns SPaG marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Malaikah (angels) are created from light, without free will: Jibril brings revelation (Surah 2:97–98), Mika’il oversees sustenance, and Izra’il takes souls at death (Surah 32:11).
  • Al-Qadr (divine decree) is one of the Sunni Six Beliefs; Sahih al-Bukhari 78:685 is the hadith anchor; Shi’a Islam stresses Adl (justice) and human free will more strongly than some Sunni accounts.
  • Akhirah includes death, barzakh, resurrection, judgement (mizan) and Jannah or Jahannam; Surah 17:49–72 is the key passage; the key contrast with Christian afterlife is the absence of purgatory and the deed-based (not atonement-based) judgement in Islam.

practice_questions.text: Outline three roles of angels (Malaikah) in Islam.
practice_questions.marks: Three discrete roles, e.g. (1) Jibril — the angel of revelation, who brought the Qur'an to Muhammad; (2) Izra'il — the angel of death, who takes the soul at death (Surah 32:11); (3) Kiraman Katibin — the two recording angels who note every human deed, which will be presented at judgement. Three separately identifiable roles.

May include: al-Qadr is one of the Six Beliefs of Sunni Islam; Allah has complete foreknowledge of all events; the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari 78:685 teaches that each person's fate is 'written' by an angel before birth; humans still have moral responsibility and are judged for their choices; Shi'a Islam stresses Adl (divine justice) and human free will. Three accurate, relevant points.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Muslim beliefs about life after death (Akhirah).
practice_questions.marks: Two developed explanations. E.g. (1) Bodily resurrection — on the Last Day Allah will raise all the dead, regardless of what has happened to the body; Surah 17 responds to sceptics asking how God can raise decomposed bones; (2) Judgement — each person's deeds are weighed on scales (mizan) and the recording angels' books are opened; Allah's mercy also plays a decisive role. Development beyond bare statements required.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Muslim beliefs about Malaikah, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: Two developed points, at least one named source. E.g. (1) Jibril is the angel of revelation — Surah 2:97–98 states he brought the Qur'an down upon the heart of Muhammad; without Jibril Muslims would have no Qur'an; (2) Izra'il is the angel of death — Surah 32:11 describes him as 'entrusted with you', taking the soul at the appointed time. 5th mark requires a named source: Surah 2:97–98 or Surah 32:11.

practice_questions.text: Outline three differences between Muslim and Catholic Christian beliefs about life after death.
practice_questions.marks: Three discrete contrasts: (1) Islam has no purgatory; Catholicism teaches purgatory as a state of purification after death; (2) In Islam, judgement is based on deeds weighed on scales (mizan) with divine mercy; in Christianity, salvation comes through faith in Christ's atoning sacrifice; (3) Islam emphasises barzakh (waiting state between death and judgement); most Christian denominations have no equivalent concept.

practice_questions.text: 'Muslim and Christian beliefs about life after death are more similar than different.' Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. FOR: both teach bodily resurrection, final judgement, and eternal destinations (Jannah/heaven, Jahannam/hell); both hold that earthly life shapes eternal destiny; both see God/Allah as just and merciful in judgement. AGAINST: purgatory (Catholic Christianity) is absent from Islam; Christianity grounds salvation in Christ's atonement — a concept absent from Islamic theology; the role of the Imam in Shi'a Islam has no Christian equivalent; Protestant Christianity (39 Articles) and Islamic teaching both reject purgatory but for different reasons. Named sources: Surah 17:49–72; 2 Corinthians 5:1–10; 39 Articles. Secure (7–9). Developing (4–6). Emerging (1–3).

knowledge_checks.q: Which Surah is the spec-named Qur'anic reference for the resurrection in Islamic teaching on Akhirah?
Which hadith collection is cited in the spec for the Islamic teaching on al-Qadr?
The angel _____ is described in Surah 32:11 as 'entrusted with you' — taking the soul at the moment of death.
In Islamic eschatology, _____ is the waiting state between death and the Day of Judgement, before the final resurrection.
Match each Islamic term to its correct description:
right: The Islamic afterlife — judgement, paradise and hell
Spiritual beings created from light, obeying Allah without free will
Divine decree — Allah's foreknowledge and sovereignty over all events

flashcard_questions.a: Angels — spiritual beings created from light, without free will, who obey Allah perfectly.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Jibril's role in Islam?
flashcard_questions.a: The angel of revelation — he brought the Qur'an to Muhammad (Surah 2:97–98).

flashcard_questions.q: What is Izra'il's role in Islam?
flashcard_questions.a: The angel of death — he takes the soul at the appointed moment (Surah 32:11).
Divine decree — Allah has foreknowledge and sovereignty over all events; humans are still morally responsible.

flashcard_questions.q: Which hadith teaches that a person's fate is 'written' before birth?
flashcard_questions.a: Sahih al-Bukhari 78:685 — provision, lifespan, deeds and final destination are recorded by an angel.

flashcard_questions.q: How does Shi'a Islam's approach to predestination differ from Sunni Islam?
flashcard_questions.a: Shi'a emphasises Adl (divine justice) and stresses human free will more strongly; a just God cannot predetermine and then punish.
The Islamic afterlife: everything after death — barzakh, resurrection, judgement, Jannah or Jahannam.
The waiting state between death and the Day of Judgement, before the final resurrection.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens at the mizan on the Day of Judgement?
flashcard_questions.a: Each person's deeds are weighed on scales — the record of the Kiraman Katibin is opened.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key contrast between Islamic and Catholic Christian afterlife beliefs?
flashcard_questions.a: Islam has no purgatory and grounds judgement in deeds and mercy; Catholicism adds purgatory and grounds salvation in Christ's atonement.

flashcard_questions.q: Which Surah challenges sceptics who doubt resurrection by asking who created them in the first place?

glossary_terms.definition: The Arabic word for angels — spiritual beings created from light, without free will, who carry out the commands of Allah perfectly and without question.
The Islamic belief that Allah has foreknowledge and sovereignty over all events — every action and outcome occurs within Allah's knowledge and decree, though humans retain real moral responsibility.
The Islamic term for the afterlife — everything that comes after death, including the Day of Judgement, paradise and hell.
The Shi'a Islamic principle of divine justice, emphasising that Allah is just and therefore humans must have genuine free will to be held accountable.
